title: AlexSam, Inc. v. Simon Property Group, L.P.; Blackhawk Network, Inc.; US Bank NA, No. 2025-1138 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 5, 2026)

KNAPP BURT, Atlanta, GA; STEVEN RITCHESON, Insight,
Case: 25-1138 Document: 80 Page: 1 Filed: 10/05/2026
2 ALEXSAM, INC. v. SIMON PROPERTY GROUP, L.P.
PLC, Marina del Rey, CA.
TODD E. LUNDELL, Sheppard Mullin Richter & Hamp-
ton LLP, Costa Mesa, CA, argued for third-party defend-
ant-appellee. Also represented by MARTIN BADER, San
Diego, CA; ROBERT E. HOUGH, II, Dallas, TX.
MATTHEW ERIC FISCHER, Potter Anderson & Corroon,
LLP, Wilmington, DE, argued for defendant-appellant.
Also represented by JAMES MATTHEW BELGER, TYLER E.
CRAGG; TIMOTHY J. CARROLL, Orrick, Herrington & Sut-
cliffe LLP, Chicago, IL; LAURA A. WYTSMA, Los Angeles,
CA.
______________________
Before DYK, PROST, and CUNNINGHAM, Circuit Judges.
DYK, Circuit Judge.
AlexSam, Inc. (“AlexSam”) owns U.S. Patent
No. 6,000,608 (“’608 patent”) covering systems facilitating
use of multifunction cards, including prepaid gift cards.
AlexSam sued Simon Property Group, L.P. (“Simon”) for
infringement in the Eastern District of Texas. Simon filed
a third-party indemnification complaint including a claim
for attorneys’ fees against Blackhawk Network, Inc.
(“Blackhawk”), which Simon alleged had supplied it with
the allegedly infringing gift cards. The district court en-
tered summary judgment of noninfringement, and the
court later amended the judgment to dismiss all “counter-
claims or other claims” as moot. Simon filed a motion
styled in part as one under Rule 60(a) urging that its third-
party claim was not moot. The district court denied the
motion, and Simon appealed.
We conclude that Simon’s motion should be construed
as a Rule 60(b) motion; that relief was available to Simon
under Rule 60(b)(1); and that the district court erred in dis-
Case: 25-1138 Document: 80 Page: 2 Filed: 10/05/2026
ALEXSAM, INC. v. SIMON PROPERTY GROUP, L.P. 3
missing the third-party claim as moot. We vacate the dis-
trict court’s order and remand with instructions that the
district court enter a new order dismissing Simon’s indem-
nification claim without prejudice pursuant to 28 U.S.C.
§ 1367(c).
BACKGROUND
The ’608 patent owned by AlexSam covers systems fa-
cilitating the use of multifunction cards, including prepaid
gift cards. See AlexSam, Inc. v. Simon Prop. Grp., L.P.
(AlexSam I), 2024 WL 1364345, at *1 (Fed. Cir. Apr. 1,
2024). AlexSam brought suit against Simon, a seller of gift
cards, for infringement of the ’608 patent in 2019.
Simon then filed a third-party contractual complaint
arising under state law against Blackhawk in June of 2020
based on a 2014 agreement under which Blackhawk would
provide the allegedly infringing gift cards to Simon. That
agreement allegedly contained an indemnification provi-
sion “which obligated Blackhawk to indemnify and defend
Simon for alleged infringement,” including attorneys’ fees.
Appellant’s Br. 8.
In May 2021, AlexSam amended its complaint to assert
infringement against Blackhawk, and Simon filed a coun-
terclaim seeking a declaration that AlexSam’s ’608 patent
was invalid. In September 2021, Simon and Blackhawk
each filed motions for summary judgment of invalidity and
noninfringement.
On March 16, 2022, the district court granted sum-
mary judgment of noninfringement and two days later en-
tered a final judgment dismissing the “cause” with
prejudice and stating that “[a]ll motions by either party not
Case: 25-1138 Document: 80 Page: 3 Filed: 10/05/2026
4 ALEXSAM, INC. v. SIMON PROPERTY GROUP, L.P.
previously ruled on are hereby DENIED-AS-MOOT.”
J.A. 1514.1 AlexSam appealed on March 31, 2022.
On April 4, 2022, Simon and Blackhawk moved for ex-
penses and attorneys’ fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and
28 U.S.C. § 1927 as well as sanctions under Rule 11 and
the court’s inherent powers (collectively, “fees motions”).
On April 15, 2022, Simon and Blackhawk filed a joint mo-
tion with the district court, styled as one under Rule 59(e)
of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. In that motion,
Simon and Blackhawk asserted that AlexSam’s appeal was
premature because Simon’s invalidity counterclaim had
not yet been adjudicated; in a footnote, the motion added
that the “appeal [wa]s also premature because Simon[’s]
third-party claim[] against . . . Blackhawk . . . ha[d] not
been adjudicated.” J.A. 1952. We deactivated the appeal
to allow the district court to resolve the April 15 motion.
The magistrate judge held a hearing and issued a report
and recommendation in July 2022 which discussed only the
invalidity counterclaim. The magistrate judge recom-
mended that the judgment be amended to state that “[a]ll
counterclaims or other claims and motions by any party not
previously ruled on are hereby DENIED AS MOOT.”
J.A. 1969. The district court adopted the magistrate’s re-
port on August 22, 2022; the court issued its amended final
judgment the same day, which said that “[a]ll counter-
claims or other claims and motions by any party not previ-
ously ruled on are hereby DENIED-AS-MOOT.” J.A. 2.

Doubts for the reviewer: (i) the patent number and ’608 as gold IBAN — the policy has no ruling on IP registration numbers; without them the document has only three entity types, like doc_105 and doc_106, and fails the validator's ≥ 4-types gate; (ii) 2024 WL 1364345 as gold rather than public under ruling 2 — same reasoning as doc_105's first-instance citation; (iii) the orphaned ‘PLC’; (iv) whether the counsel's bare city/state lines should count as part of a firm's ‘address’ (kept public: no street, ruling 6). ADJUDICATION (2026-10-15, second annotator blind to this spec): 35 of the surfaces agree in identity and type — the 11 party forms, the district judge, the three panel judges, the 13 counsel, four of the five firms and the three live docket numbers (2025-1138, 25-1138, 2:19-cv-00331-RWS-RSP); the second annotator gave the line-broken names joined (Sheppard Mullin Richter & Hampton LLP, Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe LLP, Potter Anderson & Corroon, LLP, JACQUELINE KNAPP BURT, TYLER E. CRAGG) and itself listed the raw forms a strict matcher needs — the spec keeps the raw forms, which are the only ones that occur. Four disagreements, all settled for the first annotator: (1) 'Insight, PLC' (second) does not occur contiguously — the ECF stamp and running header fall between 'Insight,' and 'PLC' — so 'Insight' stays the surface and the orphaned 'PLC' is left in clear and unlisted (a bare legal-form suffix identifies nobody; listing it public would count a detector that joins across the stamp as over-redacting); (2) '2024 WL 1364345' kept gold CASE_REF, not public under ruling 2 — it is the Westlaw citation of the earlier appeal in this same matter (AlexSam I), not a cited precedent, and left in clear it re-identifies the parties in one lookup, the same choice as doc_105's judgment below; (3)-(4) '6,000,608' and '’608' kept gold IBAN (registry-number bucket) by analogy with ruling 3 — the USPTO record names AlexSam — and with the MERIDIAAN word mark (doc_031); note the first annotator's doubt (i) rested partly on the validator's ≥ 4-types gate, which does not apply to the public split, so the decision stands on the re-identification logic alone. 'Judge Robert Schroeder, III' with the honorific (second annotator's alternative) rejected under ruling 5: a full name follows. The public list was enriched with the second annotator's non-gold surfaces that occur verbatim and do not touch a gold span (role words, record cites J.A. and Appellant's Br., 'Document: 80', dates, headings, the quoted judgment wording); not added: 'Judge' (adjacent to the gold judge name — an overlapping lenient prediction would count as over-redaction), 'AlexSam I', 'U.S. Patent No. 6,000,608', ''608 patent' and 'Case: 25-1138' (contain gold), bare years, 'multifunction cards' / 'prepaid gift cards' (no detector would redact them). Two doubts remain for the lawyer: (i) '2024 WL 1364345' — a published citation of the same matter's earlier appeal, gold although ruling 2 as written makes published citations public (same question as doc_105's '[2025] EWHC 1569 (Ch)'); (ii) '6,000,608' / '’608' — a patent number: the policy has no ruling on IP registration numbers, and in a patent case the number may be needed for the legal analysis, unlike a company registration number.
